title: Simon Ribbans Photography v. The King (Oct 2025 TCC)
subject: Tax Court application concerning filing deadlines and procedural requirements in a tax and SR&ED-related dispute.
summary: Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146, shows Canadian corporate taxpayers, including SR&ED claimants, that the Tax Court of Canada cannot extend time to object once one year and 90 days pass after a Notice of Assessment is mailed. Deemed receipt on the mailing date makes non-receipt irrelevant, so the application was denied.
metaDescription: Discover the October 2025 Tax Court of Canada ruling in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King on Canadian SR&ED tax claims.

body.text: Executive Summary and Case Background
Overview of the Proceeding and Its Place in Canadian SR&ED Practice

On October 14, 2025, the Tax Court of Canada delivered its judgment and reasons for order in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146 (Court File No. 2024-842(IT)APP), presided over by the Honourable Justice Sylvain Ouimet following a hearing in Ottawa, Ontario, on December 12, 2024. Although indexed and closely monitored within specialized Canadian Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) jurisprudence repositories, the decision does not identify the subject matter of the underlying assessments and does not adjudicate the substantive technological merits of any experimental development project under subsection 248(1) of the Canadian Income Tax Act (ITA). Rather, the ruling addresses a threshold procedural and jurisdictional failure that extinguishes a corporate taxpayer's right to contest an assessment before the Tax Court of Canada can ever evaluate the underlying substantive tax liability or credit entitlements.

In Canadian R&D tax credit practice, corporate claimants pursuing SR&ED expenditure pools under section 37 and Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) under section 127 of the ITA frequently concentrate their compliance resources on technical narratives while neglecting the strict statutory mechanics governing Notices of Assessment and Notices of Objection. Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King demonstrates the unforgiving interaction between the automated mailing machinery of the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) and the non-discretionary jurisdictional bar codified in subsection 166.2(5) of the ITA. When a corporate taxpayer fails to serve a Notice of Objection within the initial 90-day statutory window prescribed by paragraph 165(1)(b) and subsequently misses the one-year extension window under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5), the Tax Court of Canada is legally stripped of jurisdiction to grant relief—even where the taxpayer testifies in good faith that the Notices of Assessment were never physically received.
Factual Chronology and the Taxpayer's Position

The Applicant, Simon Ribbans Photography Inc., is an incorporated business whose mailing address of record with the CRA was located in Orléans, Ontario, represented at the hearing by its agent, Simon Ribbans. From October 23, 2017, through March 26, 2024, the corporation's official mailing address recorded in the CRA's electronic mainframe was 320 De La Mélodie Street, Orléans, Ontario, K1W 0H9. The validity of that corporate mailing address on file with the CRA was uncontested throughout the proceeding.

On September 13, 2022, the Minister of National Revenue (the Minister) issued Notices of Corporation Income Tax Assessment in respect of the Applicant's taxation years ending September 30, 2020, and September 30, 2021. Pursuant to paragraph 165(1)(b) of the ITA, the initial 90-day period for the corporation to serve a Notice of Objection expired in December 2022, and the subsequent one-year statutory window to apply to the Minister for an extension of time under subsection 166.1(7) expired on December 12, 2023. On January 18, 2023, the Minister issued a notice of collection notifying the corporation of outstanding tax balances owing under the assessments.

Testifying on behalf of the Applicant, Mr. Ribbans stated that the corporation never received the September 13, 2022 Notices of Assessment at its Orléans mailing address. According to the Applicant's testimony, corporate management only became aware of the underlying assessments after receiving a notice of collection in the fall of 2023. Acting upon that discovery, the Applicant served a Notice of Objection on the Minister on January 18, 2024—approximately sixteen months after the date printed on the Notices of Assessment, and thirty-seven days after the expiration of the combined one-year-and-90-day statutory extension ceiling. Because the Applicant had not previously submitted a separate extension application, the Minister treated the January 18, 2024 service of the Notice of Objection as an application for an extension of time to object.
The Minister's Challenge and Governing Statutory Framework

On March 20, 2024, the Minister formally notified the Applicant that the Notice of Objection could not be accepted as a valid objection because it had been served more than 90 days after the mailing date of the Notices of Assessment. In the same communication, the Minister refused to grant an extension of time under section 166.1 on the basis that the request was made after December 12, 2023, thereby violating the mandatory one-year limit following the expiration of the initial 90-day objection period. On March 26, 2024, the Applicant filed an application with the Tax Court of Canada pursuant to subsection 166.2(1) of the ITA seeking an order extending the time within which to serve its Notice of Objection.

The dispute was governed by an interlocking architecture of procedural and evidentiary provisions within the Canadian Income Tax Act. Under paragraph 165(1)(b), a corporate taxpayer wishing to object to an assessment must serve a written Notice of Objection on the Minister, setting out the reasons for the objection and all relevant facts, on or before the day that is 90 days after the day of sending of the Notice of Assessment. Where a corporate taxpayer misses that 90-day deadline, subsection 166.1(1) permits an application to the Minister for an extension of time, but subsection 166.1(7) expressly prohibits the Minister from granting the application unless it is made within one year after the expiration of the time otherwise limited by the ITA for serving a Notice of Objection (establishing a combined maximum period of one year and 90 days from the date of sending) and the taxpayer demonstrates that, within the objection period, it was unable to act or to instruct another to act in its name or had a bona fide intention to object, that granting the application would be just and equitable, and that the application was made as soon as circumstances permitted.

If the Minister refuses the application (or fails to respond within 90 days), subsection 166.2(1) authorizes the taxpayer to apply to the Tax Court of Canada for review. However, paragraph 166.2(5)(a) imposes an absolute statutory bar matching the Ministerial restriction: no application shall be granted by the Tax Court unless the underlying application to the Minister under subsection 166.1(1) was made within one year after the expiration of the original 90-day objection period.

To establish when the statutory countdown clock begins, the ITA deploys four powerful evidentiary and deeming mechanisms. Subsection 244(10) provides that an affidavit of a CRA officer affirming that the officer has charge of the appropriate records, has knowledge of CRA practices, has examined those records, and has verified that a notice of assessment was mailed or otherwise communicated on a specific day (and that no timely objection was received) shall be received as evidence of the statements contained therein in the absence of proof to the contrary. Subsection 244(14) creates a rebuttable legal presumption that a Notice of Assessment was mailed or sent on the date appearing on that notice. Finally, once sending is established, subsection 244(15) irrebuttably deems the assessment to have been made on the day of sending of the notice, while paragraph 248(7)(a) irrebuttably deems anything sent by first-class mail or its equivalent to have been received by the addressee on the exact day it was mailed.

body.text: The Court's Final Holding

Justice Ouimet denied the Applicant's application for an extension of time without costs. Applying settled Canadian appellate and Tax Court jurisprudence—specifically Canada v. Schafer, McClelland v. R., and Mid-Plains Contractors Ltd. v. Canada—the Court held that the statutory limitation period commences on the date the Notice of Assessment is "sent" (meaning properly addressed, stamped with proper postage, and deposited in a proper place for the receipt of mail), regardless of whether the corporate taxpayer ever physically receives or reads the document. Accepting the Crown's affidavit evidence from two CRA officers detailing the electronic generation and physical bulk mailing of the notices on September 13, 2022, the Court concluded on a balance of probabilities that the Notices of Assessment were properly mailed on that date. Because the Applicant did not serve its Notice of Objection until January 18, 2024—thirty-seven days past the December 12, 2023 deadline—subsection 166.2(5) legally barred the Tax Court from granting an extension of time.
Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Procedural and Evidentiary Deficiencies Directly Adjudicated in Simon Ribbans (2025 TCC 146)
Misconception of Non-Receipt Versus Non-Mailing Under the Four-Step Analytical Framework

The foundational legal failure in the Applicant's litigation strategy was its reliance on actual physical non-receipt as a defence against the expiration of statutory limitation periods. Mr. Ribbans contended that because the corporation never received the September 13, 2022 Notices of Assessment at its Orléans mailing address, the limitation period had not expired and the corporation remained eligible for an extension of time. Justice Ouimet systematically dismantled this contention by applying the Tax Court's four-step analytical framework governing disputed Notices of Assessment.

Under Step 1 of this framework, the taxpayer must assert that the Notice of Assessment was not mailed, which is normally accomplished either by testifying that the notice was never received (thereby raising an inference that it was not mailed) or by alleging that the notice was sent to an incorrect address through no fault of the taxpayer. Once the taxpayer satisfies Step 1—as Mr. Ribbans did through his oral testimony of non-receipt—Step 2 shifts the evidentiary burden to the Minister to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that the Notice of Assessment was in fact mailed to the proper address on file with the CRA. If the Minister discharges that burden at Step 2, Step 3 activates the rebuttable presumption under subsection 244(14) of the ITA that the notice was mailed on the date appearing on the notice, shifting the tactical burden back to the taxpayer to introduce concrete evidence proving that mailing actually occurred on a different date. Finally, once the mailing date is fixed at Step 3, Step 4 triggers two irrebuttable statutory deeming rules: subsection 244(15) deems the assessment to have been made on that mailing date, and paragraph 248(7)(a) deems the taxpayer to have received the Notice of Assessment on that exact mailing date.

As Justice Ouimet emphasized, Step 4 is not a condition for relief but a statutory consequence: it renders the fact that a taxpayer did not actually receive the Notice of Assessment in hand wholly irrelevant in law. The Applicant treated Step 1 as if it were dispositive of the entire proceeding. By offering only an uncorroborated assertion of non-receipt without advancing any forensic challenge to the CRA's electronic print logs or postal dispatch records at Steps 2 and 3, the Applicant left the Court with no legal or evidentiary basis to displace the September 13, 2022 mailing date.
Failure to Counter the Crown's Institutional Evidentiary Machinery (Subsection 244(10) Affidavits)

A critical dynamic highlighted by Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. is the profound evidentiary asymmetry between a small business taxpayer's informal administrative practices and the CRA's standardized litigation affidavits filed pursuant to subsection 244(10) of the ITA. To satisfy its burden under Step 2, counsel for His Majesty the King introduced two interlocking affidavits that traced the precise lifecycle of the Applicant's Notices of Assessment from mainframe computation to Canada Post custody.

The first affidavit, sworn by Chrisha Joseph, a CRA Litigation Officer based in Toronto, Ontario, established the electronic generation and addressing of the assessments. Ms. Joseph affirmed that she had charge of the appropriate records, possessed knowledge of CRA practices, and carefully examined the Agency's records relating to the Applicant, describing the computerized databases maintained by the CRA—specifically the Business Client Communications System (BCCS), the Electronic Communications History (ECH), and the Case Management System – Case Appeals (CSAPP). Her examination of the BCCS "Communication Item History" confirmed that the Applicant's 2020 and 2021 Notices of Assessment were processed under BCCS Cycle #000011113, which executed its cycle run on September 9, 2022, post-dated the notices for September 13, 2022, and directed them to the Applicant's registered address in Orléans, Ontario.

The second affidavit, sworn by Wade Smith, Manager of the Print to Mail Division at the Prince Edward Island Taxation Centre in Summerside, P.E.I., established the physical printing, enveloping, quality-control reconciliation, and postal deposit of the notices. Mr. Smith detailed the standardized procedures followed at the CRA's Summerside and Winnipeg "Print to Mail" sites. Once assessment files are printed, they are delivered to the inserting area and inserted into individual envelopes either manually or via an automated Bell & Howell Forerunner Inserter. Crucially, the CRA reconciles every print run against a physical job ticket, system verification reports, and trailer pages. Mr. Smith deposed that if any job fails to balance when comparing the reports, job tickets, and trailer pages, the unbalanced job is physically destroyed, reprinted, and reinserted from scratch to guarantee a balanced run. Once balanced, the envelopes are loaded into Canada Post "letterflattainers" and "monotainers" accompanied by a verified Canada Post Statement of Mailing, under strict protocols ensuring that Canada Post pick-up dates match the date printed on the assessment notices.

The Applicant did not put in issue whether the CRA officers had charge of the appropriate records and knowledge of CRA practice, and did not introduce any evidence suggesting an irregularity in BCCS Cycle #000011113 or the Summerside print-to-mail reconciliation. Consequently, the Crown readily satisfied the Mid-Plains Contractors Ltd. standard, establishing on a balance of probabilities that the notices were properly addressed, stamped with proper postage, and deposited in a proper place for the receipt of mail, and, applying subsections 244(10) and 244(14), that they were mailed on September 13, 2022.
Foreclosure of Equitable Considerations by the One-Year-and-90-Day Jurisdictional Bar

Under paragraphs 166.1(7)(b) and 166.2(5)(b) of the ITA, the Minister and the Tax Court, respectively, must evaluate equitable factors—including whether the taxpayer was unable to act or had a bona fide intention to object within the 90-day period, whether granting the application would be "just and equitable" in the circumstances, and whether the application was made as soon as circumstances permitted. However, as Justice Ouimet explained, the requirement in paragraph 166.2(5)(a) is the first condition that must be met under subsection 166.2(5), and paragraphs 166.2(5)(a) and 166.2(5)(b) are joined by the conjunctive "and". Satisfying the temporal ceiling in paragraph 166.2(5)(a)—applying within one year and 90 days of the sending date—is a mandatory condition precedent to the Court's jurisdiction. Because the Applicant missed the December 12, 2023 statutory cutoff by thirty-seven days when it served its objection on January 18, 2024, the Court was legally barred from weighing the corporation's good faith or its response to the autumn 2023 collection notice. Moreover, the evidentiary record, through Ms. Joseph's affidavit, showed that the Minister had issued a notice of collection dated January 18, 2023, addressed and sent to the same Orléans address of record—nearly eleven months before the December 12, 2023 extension window closed—although the Court made no finding as to whether that notice was received or as to the corporation's internal administrative practices, since it did not need to reach the equitable criteria in paragraph 166.2(5)(b).
Substantive Legal, Technical, and Evidentiary Failures in Canadian SR&ED Disputes

While Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King adjudicated the procedural termination of a tax dispute prior to substantive review, its prominence in Canadian SR&ED case law collections underscores a parallel reality in Tax Court of Canada litigation: SR&ED claims fail when corporate taxpayers rely on retrospective assertions rather than systematic, contemporaneous evidence. When a corporate claimant preserves its appeal rights within the 90-day objection window under paragraph 165(1)(b) to contest a CRA reassessment denying SR&ED expenditure deductions (section 37) and Investment Tax Credits (section 127) claimed on CRA Form T661, the Tax Court evaluates the claim under the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the ITA using the five-part jurisprudential test established in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (98 DTC 1839) and affirmed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA 393) and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada. Across Canadian jurisprudence, substantive SR&ED disqualifications arise from four core legal and technical deficiencies that closely mirror the evidentiary pitfalls exposed in Simon Ribbans.
Failure to Prove Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Engineering

Under the first criterion of Northwest Hydraulic, the claimant must establish on a balance of probabilities that there existed a scientific or technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures available in the public domain or within the company's existing knowledge base. Claimants routinely fail this requirement by conflating commercial novelty or functional complexity with genuine technological uncertainty. Optimizing commercial production lines, configuring off-the-shelf optical or software libraries, or resolving code defects through standard debugging procedures constitutes routine engineering. As clarified by the Tax Court in DAZZM Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 CCI 129), legitimate "system uncertainty" arises only where the combined interaction of known tools or architectures generates unpredictable performance bottlenecks or physical constraints that cannot be resolved through standard engineering practices, forcing the claimant to test unconventional strategies. When a taxpayer fails to preserve baseline documentation establishing the state of existing technology—such as prior literature reviews, benchmark analyses, and engineering feasibility studies—it cannot prove to the Court where routine engineering ended and SR&ED began.
Lack of a Structured Process of Experimentation and Hypothesis Testing

The second and third criteria of Northwest Hydraulic require the taxpayer to formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty, and to adopt a procedure that accords with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada and subsequent appellate decisions, the Federal Court of Appeal squarely rejected taxpayer arguments that adherence to the scientific method is not a mandatory requirement under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Disqualification occurs when taxpayers engage in unstructured trial-and-error tinkering—modifying mechanical parameters or software code ad hoc until a target output is achieved—without articulating a predictive causal hypothesis prior to testing, establishing objective evaluation metrics, and systematically analyzing experimental data to modify subsequent hypotheses.
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation and Uncorroborated Testimony

The fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic examines whether the taxpayer maintained a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed. Although the Tax Court confirmed in Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc. and DAZZM Inc. (applying CW Agencies) that contemporaneous documentation (such as real-time timesheets) is not an absolute legal condition sine qua non if detailed, credible alternative documentation and testimony establish the progression of the work, the Federal Court of Appeal consistently affirms SR&ED denials where a taxpayer's records are "vague," "unclear," and fail to reflect "a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result". Just as Mr. Ribbans' uncorroborated oral testimony of mail non-receipt could not overcome the CRA's BCCS logs in Simon Ribbans, a lead engineer's retrospective oral testimony at trial cannot salvage an SR&ED claim when the taxpayer lacks dated experimental logs, prototype iteration records, version-control histories, quantitative test metrics, and segregated accounting records linking claimed labour and material expenditures directly to specific experiments.
Contractual Ambiguity, Commercial Production Overlap, and Funded Research Exclusions

Under section 37 and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, a claimant's Qualified SR&ED Expenditures are reduced or excluded if the research is funded by government or non-government assistance, or if the work represents a commercial contract payment where another Canadian taxpayer is entitled to claim the SR&ED expenditure or where the contract merely requires the delivery of a commercial good or service rather than experimental development performed on behalf of the claimant. Furthermore, claimants frequently fail to isolate eligible experimental prototyping and trialing (Activity III) from pre-project financial feasibility assessments (Activity II) and post-experimentation commercial production or mass-market deployment (Activity IV). Where customer contracts mandate fixed-price delivery of commercial equipment without contractually isolating the technological risk, intellectual property vestiture, and experimental scope, the CRA characterizes the entire expenditure pool as commercial cost of goods sold rather than eligible SR&ED.

body.text: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the procedural holdings of Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 146) and the substantive SR&ED doctrines of the Tax Court of Canada into actionable compliance protocols, the following two applied case studies examine realistic Canadian corporate claimants confronting these exact legal pitfalls and detail the step-by-step remedial restructuring required to secure and defend SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.
Case Study 1: Optical Imaging and Computational Photography Hardware/Software Enterprise (Ontario)
Project Context and Identified Legal Pitfalls

LuminaMetrics Imaging Inc., a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Ottawa, Ontario, designs high-speed commercial and industrial imaging systems. During its 2023 and 2024 taxation years, the corporation undertook an R&D project to develop a sub-millimetre multi-spectral computational photography rig capable of detecting subsurface micro-fractures in moving composite aerospace panels at line speeds exceeding 4 metres per second. LuminaMetrics claimed $420,000 in qualified SR&ED expenditures (deducted under section 37) and $147,000 in enhanced 35% federal SR&ED ITCs under section 127 (alongside provincial Ontario Innovation Tax Credits) on Form T661.

LuminaMetrics confronts three compounding legal and technical pitfalls that place its entire tax credit claim at risk of forfeiture. First, on the procedural front—engaging the same deemed-mailing and deemed-receipt rules applied in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc., although the address on file with the CRA was not at issue in that case—LuminaMetrics relocated its optical studio and laboratory in suburban Ottawa during 2023 and updated its address on commercial invoices, but neglected to update its corporate mailing address in the CRA electronic mainframe or monitor its online CRA My Business Account portal. When the CRA selected the 2023 SR&ED claim for review, the Research and Technology Advisor's (RTA) query letters and the subsequent Notice of Reassessment denying the credits were mailed via a BCCS print cycle to the former studio address, leaving management unaware of the denial as the 90-day objection clock ticked down. Second, on the substantive technical front, the company's Form T661 project description conflated its commercial performance target ("capturing sharp images at 4 m/s") with technological uncertainty, while its engineers modified shutter timings and de-blurring filters through ad hoc trial-and-error without logging formal hypotheses. Third, on the contractual front, half of the development occurred while fulfilling a fixed-price equipment supply purchase order for a Canadian aerospace prime contractor, exposing the expenditures to disallowance as commercial cost of goods sold or contract-funded research under subsection 127(9).
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Restructuring Corporate Tax Governance and Statutory Deadline Controls

To eliminate the procedural vulnerability that proved fatal in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, LuminaMetrics must overhaul its corporate tax governance and CRA correspondence protocols. The corporation must enact a mandatory internal control requiring joint administrative registration on the CRA My Business Account portal for both the Chief Financial Officer and external Canadian tax counsel, with automated real-time email notifications enabled for all electronic mail, BCCS assessment cycles, and SR&ED audit communications. Any corporate relocation must trigger a documented compliance verification confirming that the address in the CRA electronic mainframe has been updated across all corporate program accounts.

Furthermore, LuminaMetrics must institute a strict 90-day protective Notice of Objection protocol governed by paragraph 165(1)(b) of the ITA. The corporate compliance calendar must calculate the 90-day objection deadline strictly from the date printed on the face of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment—recognizing that subsection 244(14) presumes mailing on that date and paragraph 248(7)(a) irrebuttably deems receipt on that exact mailing date—rather than relying on the date a physical envelope arrives. If an SR&ED dispute with a CRA reviewer remains unresolved 60 days after the printed assessment date, tax counsel must immediately serve a formal protective Notice of Objection electronically via the CRA portal, securing an automated confirmation receipt that forecloses any subsection 244(10) proof-of-no-appeal affidavit. Where a historical Notice of Reassessment is discovered belatedly through a collection notice (as the Applicant submitted occurred in the fall of 2023 in Simon Ribbans), counsel must immediately compute the one-year-and-90-day jurisdictional deadline under subsections 166.1(7)(a) and 166.2(5)(a). If the company is within that window, counsel must file a section 166.1 extension application forthwith; if the CRA alleges that the window has closed, counsel must demand disclosure of the BCCS Communication Item History, ECH records, P.E.I. or Winnipeg Print-to-Mail job tickets, trailer page balancing logs, and Canada Post Statements of Mailing to test on cross-examination whether an unrectified batch imbalance or address error undermines the Minister's proof of mailing at Step 2 or rebuts the subsection 244(14) presumption of the mailing date at Step 3.
Step 2: Re-Engineering Technical Documentation to Isolate System-Level Technological Uncertainty

To satisfy the first and fourth criteria of Northwest Hydraulic and the system-uncertainty standard articulated in DAZZM Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2024 CCI 129), LuminaMetrics must restructure its technical documentation to separate commercial functionality from underlying scientific and technological uncertainty. Before commencing experimental prototyping (Activity III), the lead optical physicist must author a dated Baseline Knowledge and Benchmark Report (Activity I) documenting prior academic literature, patent searches, and benchmark tests of off-the-shelf high-speed CMOS sensors, strobe arrays, and standard Richardson-Lucy deconvolution algorithms. This benchmark dossier must mathematically demonstrate why standard engineering solutions fail at 4 m/s due to the coupled interaction of photon starvation, sensor readout noise floor, LED thermal dissipation, and non-uniform vibrational motion blur across curved composite surfaces. By framing the Form T661 narrative around this coupled system-level conflict—where resolving one constraint through standard engineering exacerbates the others—LuminaMetrics establishes a rigorous technological uncertainty and defines the sought-after technological advancement as new knowledge governing real-time multi-spectral phase-error correction.
Step 3: Implementing Structured Experimentation and Contemporaneous Tracking

To satisfy the second, third, and fifth criteria of Northwest Hydraulic and withstand the Federal Court of Appeal's strict scientific-method scrutiny in Kam-Press Metal Products, LuminaMetrics must replace ad hoc code adjustments with a disciplined experimentation tracking system integrated into its Git version-control and Jira engineering workflows. Every experimental iteration during Activity III must be recorded contemporaneously in a structured digital laboratory record containing five mandatory elements: first, an explicit, testable technological hypothesis formulated prior to the trial (for example, hypothesizing that a custom sparse-matrix wavelet kernel executed on the FPGA will reduce deconvolution latency below 8 milliseconds while maintaining a signal-to-noise ratio above 32 decibels under induced vibrational phase shifts); second, the controlled experimental parameters and hardware configuration; third, the quantitative empirical test results, including oscilloscope traces, modulation transfer function measurements, and commit hashes; fourth, an objective engineering analysis explaining why the test succeeded or failed to match predictions (recognizing under DAZZM Inc. that conclusive negative results substantiate technological uncertainty); and fifth, the specific modification to the hypothesis for the subsequent iteration. Simultaneously, engineers must log daily hours against specific Activity III experimental hypothesis tickets, while routine mechanical enclosure design and post-validation commercial calibration (Activity IV) are segregated into non-SR&ED accounting codes.
Step 4: Restructuring Commercial Contracts to Preserve SR&ED Eligibility

To protect the $420,000 expenditure pool against commercial-production and contract-payment exclusions under subsections 37(1) and 127(9) of the ITA, LuminaMetrics must restructure its contractual agreements with the aerospace buyer. Rather than executing a single undifferentiated purchase order for custom hardware delivery, counsel must bifurcate the transaction into two distinct legal instruments or severable schedules. The commercial supply schedule must cover only the sale or licensing of a validated commercial inspection unit at fair market value, while the research and development schedule must explicitly stipulate that all underlying experimental development, optical architectures, and algorithmic source code are undertaken by LuminaMetrics on its own behalf, at its own financial and technological risk, with 100% of background and foreground intellectual property vesting exclusively in LuminaMetrics. Furthermore, the contract must include an explicit Canadian tax representation confirming that the aerospace purchaser is acquiring only a commercial end-product or license and has no contractual right or entitlement to claim SR&ED expenditures or Investment Tax Credits in respect of LuminaMetrics' engineering activities.
Case Study 2: Advanced Manufacturing and Custom Process-Engineering Firm (Quebec / Ontario Corridor)
Project Context and Identified Legal Pitfalls

ThermAlloy Process Systems Ltd. is a mid-sized Canadian custom manufacturer of industrial heat-treating and polymer-extrusion lines operating production facilities in Hawkesbury, Ontario, and Vaudreuil, Quebec. During its 2022 and 2023 taxation years, ThermAlloy initiated an experimental process-engineering project to develop a closed-loop induction heating and biopolymer co-extrusion die assembly capable of preventing thermal shear degradation when extruding recycled post-consumer bio-resins at high industrial throughput. Most of the $680,000 in claimed SR&ED expenditures consisted of shop-floor engineering salaries and raw polymer materials consumed during full-scale production-line trial runs.

ThermAlloy faces acute procedural and substantive vulnerabilities that threaten to disqualify its claim. First, on the procedural level, ThermAlloy relied entirely on an external boutique accounting firm to manage its corporate tax returns and Form T661 filings. Following a fee dispute in early 2024, ThermAlloy switched external accountants but failed to update its authorized representative records or verify where CRA paper assessments were being directed. Meanwhile, the CRA reassessed the 2022 and 2023 taxation years to deny the shop-floor SR&ED claims. Eleven months after the Notices of Reassessment were mailed via BCCS, ThermAlloy received a CRA collection notice; however, management assumed its new accountant could resolve the disallowance through informal correspondence with the CRA RTA without filing a formal Notice of Objection—allowing the roughly four months then remaining to dwindle until the company was within weeks of the absolute one-year-and-90-day jurisdictional bar under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5). Second, on the substantive level, ThermAlloy's shop-floor operators adjusted extrusion barrel temperatures and screw speeds on the live commercial line without documenting which adjustments tested scientific hypotheses versus routine commercial setup, and failed to segregate experimental scrap from sellable commercial output.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Plan
Step 1: Establishing Procedural Firewalls and Immediate Section 166.1 / 166.2 Intervention

To avert the irreversible jurisdictional bar enforced in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, ThermAlloy must immediately halt its reliance on informal accountant follow-ups, which have zero legal effect on statutory limitation periods under the Income Tax Act. Corporate tax counsel must immediately access the CRA My Business Account portal to retrieve the exact date printed on the 2022 and 2023 Notices of Reassessment from the BCCS Communication Item History and compute the 90-day objection deadline under paragraph 165(1)(b) alongside the absolute one-year-and-90-day extension ceiling under subsections 166.1(7)(a) and 166.2(5)(a).

Because the initial 90-day window has lapsed but the one-year extension window remains open for several weeks, counsel must immediately serve on the Minister a formal Application for Extension of Time under subsection 166.1(1) accompanied by the fully pleaded Notice of Objection. To satisfy the conjunctive equitable criteria in paragraph 166.1(7)(b) (and preserve the Tax Court's review jurisdiction under paragraph 166.2(5)(b) should the Minister refuse the request), the application must be supported by sworn corporate affidavits establishing that ThermAlloy maintained a continuous bona fide intention to contest the SR&ED disallowance during the transition between external accounting firms, that granting the extension is just and equitable given the third-party advisor disruption, and that the application was filed immediately upon discovering the reassessments through the collection notice. Filing prior to the expiration of the one-year-and-90-day deadline legally empowers the Tax Court of Canada to adjudicate those equitable grounds under section 166.2 rather than concluding that it cannot grant the application, as Justice Ouimet did when he denied the application in Simon Ribbans.
Step 2: Formalizing Shop-Floor Experimental Protocols and Trial Segregation

To align its commercial plant operations with the Tax Court of Canada's shop-floor SR&ED jurisprudence in CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, Abeilles Service de Conditionnement Inc., and Canafric Inc. v. The King, ThermAlloy must establish a rigorous operational boundary between commercial production and experimental development. Prior to interrupting commercial manufacturing for an experimental extrusion run, the lead process engineer must execute a dated Shop-Floor SR&ED Trial Protocol that defines the exact rheological or metallurgical uncertainty being investigated—such as non-linear viscosity degradation at shear rates exceeding 1,000 s⁻¹ caused by localized Eddy-current thermal spikes in the induction manifold—and states the specific hypothesis being tested by modifying the die land geometry or induction pulse-width modulation frequency.

During the designated experimental window, the line must be formally logged out of commercial production in the plant's Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) system. Automated Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) telemetry—capturing real-time melt pressure, barrel temperature profiles, screw torque, and shear-rate curves—must be archived and stamped with the Trial Protocol identifier to corroborate the systematic testing of the hypothesis. All bio-resin extruded during the trial window must be physically quarantined as experimental test specimens, subjected to laboratory tensile and molecular-weight degradation analysis, and accounted for strictly as materials consumed or transformed in SR&ED so that no commercial inventory costs contaminate the Form T661 expenditure pool.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Evidentiary Synthesis for CRA Audit and Tax Court Readiness

To ensure that the evidentiary record satisfies both the CRA's Research and Technology Advisors during administrative review and the Tax Court of Canada under the fifth criterion of Northwest Hydraulic, ThermAlloy must transition from retrospective year-end claim preparation to quarterly contemporaneous synthesis. At the close of each fiscal quarter, the engineering and finance teams must compile a unified SR&ED Evidentiary Dossier containing the signed Shop-Floor SR&ED Trial Protocols, the raw PLC telemetry plots, the laboratory failure-analysis reports showing the logical progression from experimental premise to result, CAD revision histories of the modified induction dies, and payroll time-cards linking specific shop-floor operators and engineers to the exact hours of each experimental run. When the CRA Appeals Officer or RTA reviews the Notice of Objection, ThermAlloy can present an indexed documentary record that proves each of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria on a balance of probabilities while resting on an unassailable procedural foundation under sections 165, 166.1, and 166.2 of the Income Tax Act.
Conclusions and Practice Directives for Canadian Tax Advisors

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 146) delivers an unmistakable mandate to Canadian corporate taxpayers, engineering executives, and SR&ED tax advisors: substantive scientific merit is entirely moot if statutory procedural deadlines are breached. Because the Crown can reliably establish the mailing of a Notice of Assessment on a balance of probabilities under subsection 244(10) by filing standardized officer affidavits detailing BCCS electronic cycles and P.E.I. or Winnipeg Print-to-Mail reconciliation controls, the statutory presumption of the mailing date under subsection 244(14) and the irrebuttable deeming of receipt on the day of mailing under paragraph 248(7)(a) operate ruthlessly against taxpayers who rely on physical mail delivery or informal accountant assurances. Once the combined one-year-and-90-day period under subsections 166.1(7)(a) and 166.2(5)(a) expires, the Tax Court of Canada is legally stripped of jurisdiction to grant an extension of time regardless of good faith or actual non-receipt. Consequently, defensible Canadian R&D tax credit governance requires pairing rigorous, contemporaneous Northwest Hydraulic experimental documentation with continuous CRA My Business Account digital monitoring and disciplined 90-day protective objection protocols.

outcome: Application dismissed; court enforced statutory filing deadlines, noting strict compliance with time limits is mandatory.
